subject.resolution_note: The name 'gogent' is heavily overloaded: GitHub search returns 50 repos named gogent (plus gogentic/gogento variants). The parent issue title 'gogent: Go Agent Infrastructure' matches ONLY tltre/gogent, whose own tagline is 'Gogent — Go agent infrastructure'. All other gogent repos are unrelated projects (log-analysis worker, Lua-scripted agent, Godot plugin, Magento Go client) and must not be conflated in the article.
subject.language: Go only (838,566 bytes of Go; no other language)

competitors.name: Eino (ByteDance CloudWeGo)
key_points: Most-starred Go LLM framework: 13,219 stars, 1,119 forks, last push 2026-09-29
Typed component graph orchestration (ChatModel/Tool/Retriever/ChatTemplate) with automatic stream concat/merge/boxing between nodes
ChatModelAgent runs the ReAct loop internally; DeepAgent adds planning + sub-agent delegation
Production-hardened at ByteDance (Doubao/TikTok): circuit breakers, exponential backoff, dead-letter queues, bulkhead isolation
Still 0.x with frequent alphas (v0.9.20 Sept 2026, v0.10.0 alpha) and documented API churn; eino-ext holds provider components separately
Module declares go 1.18 — the lowest toolchain bar among the major Go frameworks

competitors.name: Google ADK for Go
key_points: Official Google first-party SDK: 8,837 stars, 1,024 forks — highest commit velocity of the group
v0.1.0 Nov 2025, 1.0 Mar 2026, google.golang.org/adk/v2 Jun 2026; v2.4.0 as of Sept 2026
Agent-only design: everything is an agent, workflow agent, or tool — no vanilla generation primitive, no flow abstraction
First-party sequential/parallel/loop workflow agents, sessions, memory, artifacts, A2A protocol, MCP toolsets, tool confirmation, embedded web UI
Gemini-first with strong Vertex AI / Cloud Run / GKE gravity; non-Gemini via OpenAI-compatible endpoints
Requires the newest toolchain (Go 1.26.6+ in the v2 line) — highest floor of the mainstream options

competitors.name: tRPC-Agent-Go
key_points: 1,836 stars, 321 forks; positioned as 'LangGraph in Go' with GraphAgent state graphs, checkpoints and interrupts
ADK-style mental model without the GCP gravity — AG-UI frontends, Agent Skills, evaluation and OpenTelemetry out of the box
Graph workflows + tools + memory + A2A + MCP in one framework
Smaller community and a large API surface are the documented trade-offs

competitors.name: Genkit Go (Google/Firebase)
key_points: 6,463 stars; official first-party Go SDK shipped Aug 2024, reached 1.0 Sept 2025, v1.13.1 as of Sept 2026 (~monthly minor releases)
Three abstraction levels in one SDK: direct model calls, typed flows, and an agents package (still experimental)
Middleware layer (retry, fallback, tool approval, filesystem, skills) wraps any of the three levels
Best-in-class Dev UI local trace explorer; OTel pipeline traces all three levels
The polished Genkit Monitoring dashboard is Google-Cloud-only; requires Go 1.25+

competitors.name: Microsoft Agent Framework for Go
key_points: 634 stars, extremely active (pushed 2026-10-01); public preview, evolving outside the core MAF upstream
Graph-based workflows: sequential, concurrent, group collaboration, conditional routing, subworkflows, checkpointing, human-in-the-loop, time-travel
Broad ecosystem surface: Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, MCP, A2A, AG-UI, GitHub Copilot SDK
Explicit Go/.NET parity gaps: handoff orchestration, declarative agents, RAG, CodeAct and functional workflows not implemented in Go; DevUI absent
Does not configure telemetry collection by default

competitors.name: gogentic (name-neighbour, listed to prevent conflation)
key_points: 4 stars, 4 forks, forked from langchaingo; 'LLM Agents in Go'
Stronger tool/assistant abstractions, schema generation, Agent Skills (SKILL.md with progressive disclosure), MCP client+server

Agentic use is still nascent: only 17% of Go developers primarily use AI tools as unsupervised agents, though 40% occasionally try agentic modes

Anthropic's production finding: the strongest agent implementations use simple composable patterns rather than frameworks; Zep puts the core agent loop at roughly 40 lines of Go and reports most Go teams skip frameworks entirely
Go ships as a single static binary and goroutines start at ~2KB, so a Go agent service typically uses 3-5x less memory than an equivalent Python service
MCP: 10K+ active public servers cited by Anthropic (Dec 2025); 15,926 GitHub repos with the mcp-server topic on 2026-05-24; official MCP SDKs see close to half-a-billion downloads per month

MCP spec 2026-07-28 is the largest revision since launch: it goes stateless (removes the initialize handshake and protocol-level session), adds MCP Apps and a Tasks extension, and aligns auth closer to OAuth/OIDC

MCP has a credible enterprise foothold but not ubiquity: 41% of surveyed software organizations are in limited or broad production with MCP servers (Stacklok 2026); 'over 10,000 active public MCP servers' is the vendor-cited figure; 30% of software vendors expected to publish their own MCP server
Eino (ByteDance) is the most-starred Go LLM framework at 13,219 stars; Google ADK Go has 8,837 stars and the highest commit velocity of the mainstream Go agent frameworks
tltre/gogent itself: 3 stars, 1 fork, 0 open issues, 0 open PRs, 125 commits, 1 contributor, 1 release (v0.15.0), MIT — a single-author pre-1.0 project published 2026-08-17

angles: Name disambiguation first: 'gogent' returns 50 GitHub repos, ~8 of them Go agent projects, and the top search hit (tobalo/gogent at 15 stars) is a completely different log-analysis worker. Establish which gogent this review is about before any verdict.

'Harness, not library' is the real differentiator: gogent explicitly refuses to own your agent logic and instead ships the operational layer — daemon, subprocess isolation, port allocation, crash recovery, centralized tool registry, least-privilege manifests, sandbox routing, credentials, OTel. That is a genuine gap in the Go ecosystem, where Eino/Genkit/ADK are all in-process libraries.

Honest scale check: 3 stars, 1 contributor, 125 commits from a single author, one release. This is a review of a well-architected solo pre-1.0 project, not a production-ready competitor to Eino or ADK Go — say so plainly.

The daemon/subprocess model is the most interesting design decision and also the biggest operational cost: components can each be forked as their own OS process, the daemon crash-isolates the agent via PID probing, but this means HTTP API on :9090, port files, a gRPC ToolService hop for every tool call, and harder debugging.

Architecture documentation is unusually strong for a 3-star project: seven ADRs (agent/daemon/tool/provider/sandbox/contextmanager/observability) that document rejected alternatives and trade-offs — worth reading even by people who never install it.

'gogent' as a keyword almost certainly signals AI-generated or templated naming churn: 50 near-identical repos across 2024-2026, most abandoned within weeks (canergulay, asabla, rxcrystal, sceneryback, hobbestherat all ≤1 star). The article's keyword targets a crowded, mostly dead namespace.

Timing tension with the market: only 11% of Go developers work with ML models/tools/agents, 78% build no AI features, and Anthropic's own guidance and Zep's field report both say most Go teams skip frameworks for a ~40-line loop. A review must answer 'why this framework at all' before 'is it good'.

outline: H2: What Gogent Actually Is (and Which Gogent This Is) — disambiguate the 50-repo name collision, identify tltre/gogent, one-paragraph positioning as an 'agent application harness'
H2: The Core Idea: Infrastructure, Not Business Logic — the harness-vs-library distinction; what gogent deliberately does not do; quote the README's own framing
H2: Architecture Walkthrough — the daemon/app/OTel topology; nine-component system; topological component init; where the gRPC and HTTP boundaries sit
H2: The Daemon and Subprocess Model — gogent run vs gogent serve; OS-subprocess isolation, port allocation, PID-probing crash recovery; why the daemon dying does not kill running agents

H2: Tools, MCP, and Least Privilege — daemon-side ToolRegistry, manifest-based declarative authorization, server.tool sub-tool expansion, process/http MCP drivers, 30s Ping health checks with auto-restart after three failures, three-level sandbox routing (per-tool to app default to daemon default)

H2: Providers, Credentials, and Runtime Switching — OpenAI and DeepSeek native engines plus 10+ OpenAI-compatible vendors; dynamic model-list fetching; app-scoped credentials.yaml with masked keys and fsnotify hot-reload; /provider and /model switching in the REPL

H2: Observability and Context Management — three-level spans (agent.run to agent.llm.generate to tool.exec) with tool-execution audit events exported over OTLP gRPC; the v0.16.x context-compression work on master beyond the v0.15.0 tag
H2: How Gogent Compares — a table against Eino, Google ADK Go, tRPC-Agent-Go, Genkit Go and Microsoft Agent Framework for Go on layer, stars, process model, MCP, sandbox, observability and maturity

H2: Honest Limitations — 3 stars, one contributor, single release, pre-1.0, Go 1.25.5 floor, not published on pkg.go.dev, no community, Chinese-first design docs, daemon operational overhead, Windows/Unix process shims, no hosted deployment story

H2: Who Should Actually Use It — three concrete profiles (self-hosting teams that want multi-agent process isolation on one box, infra engineers who want a tool/MCP gateway with least-privilege manifests, architects studying a reference daemon design) and the profile that should pick Eino, ADK Go or Genkit instead

H2: Verdict — score-style verdict with an explicit 'promising design, unproven project' framing; what would change the verdict (a second contributor, a pkg.go.dev release, v1.0, adoption beyond the author)
research_notes: Type 'review' — this is a single-project review, not a comparison or best-of. The comparison section is context, not the spine.
Do NOT describe gogent as a popular or widely-used framework. Every adoption metric available says otherwise (3 stars, 1 contributor, 1 release, 0 forks, 0 issues, 0 PRs).
All repository facts verified via the GitHub REST API (authenticated `gh api`) on 2026-10-01. Star counts are a point-in-time snapshot.

The default branch is 'master' and it is ahead of the v0.15.0 tag: master carries v0.16.x work (contextmanager compression engine, remote model-spec catalog) that is unreleased. Note the lag explicitly.
https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/tltre/gogent returns HTTP 404 — the module is not indexed on pkg.go.dev (consistent with its age and lack of adoption). Do not link readers there.
The repo has only one release page entry (v0.15.0) even though the README's 'Since v0.12.2' comment implies earlier internal versioning; treat v0.15.0 as the only public tag.
No browser/Playwright fallback was needed: the GitHub API, Go module proxy, and curl/web_extract on article URLs all returned 200 throughout.
